close_reason: Added new() constructors to all 12 public structs (NDay, RecurrenceRule, Location, VirtualLocation, Link + with_href/with_blob_id, Relation, Participant, OffsetTrigger, AbsoluteTrigger, Alert, TimeZoneRule, TimeZone) plus Default impls for Location, Link, Relation (the three with no mandatory fields). Constructors take only the spec-mandatory fields as args; all optional fields default to None and at_type is set to the wire discriminator literal. Chose constructor-with-mandatory-args over global Default-with-empty-strings because empty-string defaults for mandatory fields like NDay.day or RecurrenceRule.frequency would be wire-invalid. Added two tests: constructors_set_at_type_to_wire_discriminator (probes all 12) and link_constructors_satisfy_source_invariant. cargo test + clippy -D warnings clean.
description:
**Contract risk**: every public struct in this crate carries
`#[non_exhaustive]` (workspace policy) but the crate ships no `Default`
impl, no `new()` constructor, and no builder pattern for any of them.
Combined, this means external callers literally cannot construct any
of `NDay`, `RecurrenceRule`, `Location`, `VirtualLocation`, `Link`,
`Relation`, `Participant`, `OffsetTrigger`, `AbsoluteTrigger`, `Alert`,
`TimeZoneRule`, or `TimeZone` from outside the crate. The only
construction path is `serde_json::from_value(...)` round-trip.

**What goes wrong for callers**:
- Any consumer of `jmap-calendars-types` or future `jmap-tasks-types`
  that wants to BUILD a wire-bound object server-side (e.g. constructing
  a `CalendarEvent` to send to a client) cannot write
  `RecurrenceRule { at_type: "RecurrenceRule".into(), frequency: ... }`.
  They have to write `serde_json::from_value(json!({...}))` for every
  sub-object — round-tripping their data through JSON just to satisfy
  the type system.
- Test fixtures in downstream crates inherit the same constraint.
  The internal tests in this crate can construct directly because they
  ARE the defining crate; external tests cannot.
- Adding new optional fields (the whole point of `#[non_exhaustive]`)
  is a non-breaking change, but ONLY if callers had a way to
  construct in the first place — which they don't. So
  `#[non_exhaustive]` is doing no work today; it only starts
  protecting once constructors exist.

**Fix shape** (non-breaking, additive):
- Add `impl <Type> { pub fn new() -> Self { ... at_type set correctly ... } }`
  for each struct, defaulting all `Option` fields to `None` and any
  mandatory non-Option fields to their natural empty value
  (`String::new()`, `HashMap::new()`).
- OR implement a manual `Default` per struct that wires `at_type` to
  the correct discriminator string, since auto-derived `Default` would
  give `at_type = String::new()` and produce wire-invalid values.

Caveats: a naive `new()` for `VirtualLocation` (with mandatory `uri`)
and `Participant` (with mandatory `roles`) would still leave the
caller with an invalid object — but at least it gives them a
starting point to .uri = / .roles.insert(...) from.

**Workspace-policy note**: this is the same friction every other
type-crate in the workspace inherits. If the fix lands here, it
should propagate to the canonical-template sweep (mail-types,
chat-types, etc.). File as workspace-architectural if treated that
way; otherwise this crate is a fine place to start.
title: Public structs are #[non_exhaustive] but ship no Default impl or constructor methods — callers cannot construct any of these types in Rust
